events.title: The word brought home to Achadh àrsaidh
events.body: The second of the two Achadh àrsaidh boats that met the strangers' ships off the north-west cape turns home and brings the word to its households, while Lachlann Odhar's boat leads the strangers' ships south toward Cuan shean. Achadh àrsaidh is the first place on the island to hear of the strangers, and it hears of them from its own fishers.

events.title: Lachlann Odhar leads the ships down the coast
events.body: Lachlann Odhar steers south from the north-west cape the length of a winter day, past the empty headlands of the north-west, with the strangers' ships shortening sail to keep behind him. He runs his boat up the shingle at Cuan shean after dark and wakes the custodians.

events.title: The ships stand off Cuan shean in the westerly weather
events.body: A run of westerly gales keeps Na Trì Longan standing off and on beyond the bar of Cuan shean for many days. The town watches them from the dunes, and the custodian Oighrig nic Leòid forbids any boat to put off to them or any fire to be lit on the strand.

events.title: The rider from Cuan shean reaches Cathair dhearg
events.body: A rope-maker's son of Cuan shean rides the valley road to the capital in a day with Oighrig nic Leòid's letter on the ships. The clerk of the council reads it standing. The council's answer, two days later, bids Cuan shean feed the strangers, keep them apart and decide nothing.

events.title: Oighrig nic Leòid gives water on the shingle
events.body: Edmund Harrow wades ashore at Cuan shean with an empty cask, and the custodian Oighrig nic Leòid gives him and his eleven men water from the town well under the old law of the shore. She has seven casks filled and refuses anything more on her own word.

events.title: Three of Harrow's men buried above the tide-line
events.body: Three of the strangers, sick from the long voyage, die on the strand below the dunes at Cuan shean. Their own people bury them above the tide-line with a reading from a book and kneeling on the sand, while the town's children watch from the dunes.

events.title: Harrow's men mend nets on the dunes
events.body: Recovered from their sickness, the strangers penned below the dunes at Cuan shean begin mending the fishers' nets spread on the strand, unasked. The fishers learn from them a flat knot that does not slip, and call it the strangers' knot.

events.title: Buttons traded for fish on the strand
events.body: The first trade between the island and the strangers begins on the strand at Cuan shean, yellow-metal coat buttons for fish. The custodians forbid it twice and it goes on behind the dunes; at last Oighrig nic Leòid lets it be, and the fishwives wear the buttons on cords.

events.title: Manannan's priests keep the tide-prayer through the forty days
events.body: Through the forty days the strangers are fed below the dunes, the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say their prayer to keep the sea shut at every tide without missing one. The harbour scribe enters their number each week, nine, with the weather and the thinness of Ceò Mhanannain.

events.title: Oighrig nic Leòid's letter to the council from her sickbed
events.body: From her bed at Cuan shean Oighrig nic Leòid writes to the council that she gave the strangers water under the law of the shore and nothing more on her own word, and that a leave given in the roll cannot be ungiven. She asks that it be read before the vote. The clerk notes it received.

events.title: The strangers sheltered in the net-lofts
events.body: With the autumn gales the custodians of Cuan shean let the strangers off the open strand into the net-lofts along the harbour. The ships lie in the harbour with their yards sent down and a few hands aboard. The roll enters the lofts as a shelter for the winter and no leave.

events.title: Oighrig nic Leòid falls ill
events.body: At Samhain the custodian of Cuan shean takes a cough that goes into her chest, and by an Dùbhlachd she cannot leave her bed. Custodians riding up to the council at Cathair dhearg stop at her bedside on the way.

events.title: The leave read on the strand at Cuan shean
events.body: A custodian of Cuan shean reads the council's leave to the strangers from an upturned boat on the strand, with a stranger who has learned some words in the net-lofts putting it into his own tongue. The strangers cheer three times and begin to send their ships' yards back up.

events.title: The struck line in the council roll
events.body: Bidden to strike from the council's roll the old sailors' saying about the quarter of the sea, the clerk at Cathair dhearg strikes it and writes beneath the striking what he was told to strike, so that the next clerk should know. The saying stands in the roll so, struck and unanswered.

events.title: Lachlann Odhar's words at the harbour wall
events.body: Going home at last to Achadh àrsaidh in an Gearran, Lachlann Odhar stands on the harbour wall at Cuan shean and says aloud that the ships came out of the quarter Cabhlach an Scaraidh sailed into. Nobody on the harbour answers him, and he puts out for the north.

events.title: The humans pray in a sail-loft at Cuan shean
events.body: On the day the strangers keep for their god a sailmaker of Cuan shean lends them his loft against the rain. They kneel on the sailcloth, the captain with the rest, while a priest reads from a book; they light no fire and burn nothing. Two priests of Manannan watch from the stair and go down to the water to say their own prayer. It is the first entry of the humans at prayer under a roof.

events.title: Wren and the priests come up to Cathair dhearg
events.body: Two priests of the humans and a boy ride up from Cuan shean on ponies of the town, a long day's road, and come over the bridge at dusk soaked through. The council lodges them in a house below the temple and gives them a long room on the east side of the hall. The younger priest, Samuel Wren, coughs in the damp of the lake country.

events.title: Crìosd and an Eaglais written in the council roll
events.body: In the same season as an Tìr Thall the clerk of Comhairle a' Chùraim enters the name of the strangers' one god as the island hears it, Crìosd, and calls their faith an Eaglais, after the word their priests use of the whole company of their believers. They are the first words of the humans' tongue that the island takes and keeps.

events.title: The keeping of the word-list given to Gormshuil nic Fhearchair
events.body: The humans' priests ask Cuan shean for someone to trade words with them at a table, and Cuan shean sends to the capital. Tormod mac Ailein calls Gormshuil nic Fhearchair, who sits on the council for Clann Fhearchair and writes the best hand in the hall, and the council gives her the keeping of the island's side of the list. Her niece Muireall is to make the fair copy.

events.title: Wren sets his months against the moons
events.body: Wren draws the twelve months of the humans' sun-year as a wheel, and Gormshuil nic Fhearchair gives him the island's moons from Samhnas round to the stags' moon. He writes each moon's name beside the month it most nearly matches. For Eadrach, the between-moon, he finds no place, and writes it outside the wheel with the humans' mark of a question.

events.title: Wren names the fuel of his own country
events.body: Over a brazier of peat in the long room Wren shows by signs that his people burn peat too, and also a black stone dug from under the ground, which they burn in every house. Gormshuil nic Fhearchair writes his word for it and, in the Dia-thìris column, the black stone the humans dig in their own country and burn on their hearths.

events.title: Muireall copies the first leaf
events.body: In the gap-moon Gormshuil nic Fhearchair gives her loose sheets to her niece Muireall to copy fair into a book for Clann Fhearchair, and orders the colours set first, before cup and bread, alone on the first leaf with room left at the foot. Muireall copies the forty words in her young, careful hand and stops at the right-hand column, where the humans' side has one word to give.

events.title: The basket of broken coal on the table
events.body: In the wolf-moon Gormshuil nic Fhearchair takes a double handful from the capital's measure for the shrines and tips it on the table before Samuel Wren in the winter sun. She names forty colours at the breaks. Wren writes some of them, then stops, turns a piece in the light and gives one word for the whole heap. She waits for him to ask for hers; he holds up a candle.

events.title: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair begins the humans' letters
events.body: Since Wren cannot learn her colours, Gormshuil nic Fhearchair asks him by signs to teach her his letters. He writes them across a sheet of his white paper, large and small, and her name beneath as he hears it, and she copies it stroke by stroke. By the end of the spring she can spell out a line of his word-list, and finds his one word under her colours.

events.title: The first bargains entered in the council roll
events.body: At the moon of the bright fire the strangers' iron, glass, lamp-oil and paper come up to the capital's market, and wool, hides, salt fish and dyed cloth go down to Cuan shean. Comhairle a' Chùraim enters the first bargains in its roll, fleece for knife and cloth for glass, with both prices in the island's reckoning. The measure is good on both sides.

events.title: The copy of the list sent to the loft at Muileann chaol
events.body: Having watched the humans burn their spoiled paper, Gormshuil nic Fhearchair has Muireall make a second fair copy of the whole list, the colours first and the note at the foot of the first leaf. She seals it in an oak chest with the seal of Clann Fhearchair and sends it east with the carriers to the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais, where nothing is burned.

events.title: The custodians' clerk keeps a slate beside Pike's book
events.body: The custodians of the capital shore set a clerk on a stool by the door of the humans' post at Ros dhomhain. He keeps his own tally of the day's goods on a slate in the old strokes, and each evening he and Thomas Pike read their two counts aloud and find them level.

events.title: Goods carted from Cuan shean to the post
events.body: In the first weeks of the post every bale and cask goes between the strangers' ships at Cuan shean and the counter at Ros dhomhain by cart over the moor road, two days each way. The carters of Cuan shean charge by the creel, and Harrow goes to the pilots of Caol leathan for a way by water.

events.title: The pilots' double toll entered as fair
events.body: The pilots of Caol leathan go over the smallest of Harrow's hulls and name twice the toll of a Dia-thìreach boat for bringing her up the Abhainn gheal. Harrow is angry. Pike enters the price in the post's tally-book and writes beside it that it is fair, since the pilots know the shallows.

events.title: The gift of paper to Cathair naomh
events.body: Paying the custodians of Cathair naomh for their wool in paper and ink, Pike adds a quire of his own writing-paper uncounted. It is the one line of the post's first tally-book that he does not balance, and he marks it as a gift.

events.title: Harrow sails north-about with three hulls
events.body: At the end of an Lùnastal Edmund Harrow sails from Cuan shean for an Tìr Thall with all three hulls, north-about, carrying hides and dyed cloth. He leaves Thomas Pike at Ros dhomhain with four men, the loft, the tally-book and the goods not yet traded.

events.title: The ships' smith at the forge in Cathair dhearg
events.body: A smith off Harrow's ships, sent up by Pike, comes to the smiths' lane below Drochaid Cathair dhearg and works through the autumn at the forge of Gilleasbuig Gobha. Having no words in common, the two smiths agree on the colours of hot iron.

events.title: Gilleasbuig Gobha's first tempered blade
events.body: In the last days of an Dùbhlachd Gilleasbuig Gobha tempers his first blade alone at his forge in Cathair dhearg, a knife of the humans' bar-iron drawn to the straw next the brown. It cuts hide that the old bronze knives only bruise. He gives it to his wife Sìne.

events.title: Iron hoes on the capital's fields
events.body: Through am Faoilleach and am Màrt the smiths of Cathair dhearg forge iron hoes, and the farmers above the lake pay for them with their old bronze hoes, brought down in sacks. Some of the bronze hoes bear the marks of the fields they worked.

events.title: The bells of Cathair dhearg cast from the hoes
events.body: At the asking of the custodians, Gilleasbuig Gobha and two smiths of the lane melt down the bronze hoes in a mould-pit behind his forge and cast four bells. They hang in the market gate, at the bridge and at the temple of Cathair dhearg, and are first rung together at Lùnastal.

events.title: The trading house's letter read at the post
events.body: Toward the end of an Dàmhair Thomas Pike reads at his counter the letter Harrow has brought from the trading house over the sea, aloud in both tongues. It asks what else the island has: timber, tin, copper, lead, and what the rocks hold. Gilleasbuig Gobha hears it read.

events.title: Oighrig nic Leòid witnesses the setting of the leg
events.body: Old and ill, Oighrig nic Leòid, custodian of Cuan shean, is carried to the fisherman's house to watch Jonas Tull break and set the crooked leg again. Told he has done it eleven times and nine have walked, she says that nine of eleven is more than the island has, and writes the debt in the roll.

events.title: Pike's first two years balanced
events.body: In the first days of an Giblean Thomas Pike closes the tally-book of the post at Ros dhomhain on its second year. Over two nights he and the custodians' clerk go through every line of both years, book against slate, and the two counts stand level.

events.title: Pike writes home of the island's coal
events.body: Answering the trading house, Thomas Pike writes of the island's timber, salt, wool, hides and smiths, and that it has copper, tin and some silver. Having held a piece from a custodian's hearth to the window, he writes that the island has coal of a middling sort, and much of it.

events.title: Gilleasbuig Gobha forges a hinge for Pike's chest
events.body: Gilleasbuig Gobha makes a new hinge of the strangers' bar-iron for the iron-bound chest under Pike's counter, where letters for over the sea are kept. He tempers it to the blue and will take nothing for the work. Pike's letter on the coal goes over the sea in that chest.

events.title: Carpenters and a cooper come ashore at Baile dhìreach
events.body: A boat of the humans' post rows down from Cuan shean deep with sawn plank and grounds on the shingle north of the quay at Baile dhìreach. Seven men of Harrow's ships come ashore, the carpenter William Rook and the cooper Samuel Hale among them, seeking a sheltered beach for a slip where the small craft of the post may be mended and built.

events.title: The rule of the shingle read to the strangers
events.body: The shingle above the wrack-line at Baile dhìreach is held in keeping for the whole town and may not be sold. Seonag nic Aoidh of the salt-house reads the town's rule to the strangers on the shore: the well drawn in turn, no fire on the shingle in the herring season, no hammer on the rest-nights. Rook says his men will keep it.
